The Euclid-Euler theorem. This theorem establishes a complete and elegant characterization of even perfect numbers. An even number is perfect—equal to the sum of its proper divisors—if and only if it is of the form two to the power p minus one times two to the power p minus one, where two to the power p minus one is a prime Mersenne number. This single theorem beautifully unites two classical subjects: perfect numbers and Mersenne primes.

Here's what you need to know. An even number n is perfect exactly when it has the form two to the power p minus one times M sub p, where M sub p, which equals two to the power p minus one, is a Mersenne prime. Euclid proved the forward direction way back in the Elements: if two to the power p minus one is prime, then two to the power p minus one times two to the power p minus one is perfect. Euler later proved the converse: every even perfect number must have this exact form. The first four perfect numbers illustrate this beautifully: 6 equals two times three, 28 equals four times seven, 496 equals sixteen times thirty-one, and 8128 equals sixty-four times one hundred twenty-seven. Each of these is constructed exactly as the theorem predicts. The theorem's implications are profound: finding new Mersenne primes is equivalent to finding new even perfect numbers, which is why mathematicians conduct intensive computational searches for Mersenne primes. It's one of the most satisfying connections in number theory, where two seemingly unrelated types of numbers turn out to be perfectly paired.
